newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee rallies again, copper hits year-high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee rallies again, copper hits year-high.

text.p: The world price of coffee jumped ahead on Wednesday as producer countries said they would maintain export quotas for another year.
Elsewhere in the commodity markets, copper hit a new year high for the second day running on continued tight supply.

The price of the high quality arabica coffee beans traded in New York rallied sharply after the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) announced export quotas would be held for another year.
The front month July contract jumped to $2.52 before easing a couple of cents as the profit-takers blew the froth of its most recent gains.
The benchmark July contract for the London-traded robusta beans failed to match New York and closed up 15 cents at $2,090 a tonne.
The ACPC agreed to cap exports for the 12 months from July 1 at 52.75 million bags to try to lock in gains from a rally that took arabica futures to a 20-year high at $2.80 last week.

There was also some nervous buying of futures on Wednesday on reports of colder weather heading for Brazil, the biggest exporter, where winter brings a risk of frost damage, while another big U.S. roaster has raised its retail price.

On Tuesday, Maxwell House Coffee Co, a division of Philip Morris' Kraft Foods, said it raised its standard 13-ounce can of regular and decaffeinated ground coffees by 30 cents to $3.36 and $4.06 respectively.
The price hike came a day after Procter & Gamble Co unit Folgers Coffee Co announced an identical increase.
Both roasters, the two largest in the U.S., have boosted the retail price by almost 50 percent, or $1.10, since February.
A dearth of copper stocks in northern Europe kept premiums for physical delivery of the red metal firm.

"Everything in northern Europe is getting firmer because of the shortage of material," said one trader. The physical market was especially tight in Britain where London Metal Exchange warehouses had stood empty since March 24.
The price of three-months delivery LME copper hit a one-year high of $2,518 a tonne befrore easing to close $2 down from the open at $2,504.

But some traders said they expected the metal to top out at current levels. "It can't go any higher, because then people will start shipping metal into the U.K. from other European warehouses," one trader said.
In Europe overall, LME copper stocks were also down to around 75,000 tonnes this week, compared to close to 200,000 tonnes at the start of the year.
Cocoa fell below 1,000 pounds sterling a tonne mark despite comment by the commodity minister of Ivory Coast, the biggest seller, that there would be a deficit this year.
Guy-Alain Gauze said he would go to Brazil at the end of June for talks on how to improve prices and that he was thinking of holding back sales.
"The prices are good but we are looking to improve them," he said.

The price of gold closed at $342.70, down just 10 cents an ounce as early buying failed to hold and platinum group metals (PGMs) which hit highs earlier in the week on shortages from Russia, were firm but static.

Benchmark IPE North Sea Brent crude dipped back into negative territory on the back of selling in New York to hover just under the $20 a barrel. Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade were little changed despite some Egyptian buying.
